title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which fraudulent emails were sent to public figures using the name and identity of a real, well-known broadcaster. The failure is not in a single AI product but in the use of AI-assisted text generation as a tool to make deceptive outreach more convincing and cheaper to produce at scale. The scam operated at the point of initial contact, before any institutional system could intervene, because the emails mimicked legitimate booking inquiries closely enough to pass a first read.

What made the impersonation harder to detect was the personalization: messages referenced targets' actual work and proposed plausible interview topics. A human-written mass scam of this specificity would have been costly to run, and cybersecurity experts cited in the reporting say AI has reduced that cost significantly. The red flags that allowed one recipient to identify the fraud, an unofficial Gmail address and a payment request, were present but required the target to look past an initially credible message.

What is not established is which specific AI system or systems were used, whether any individual or group has been identified as responsible, and whether any target sent money.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been sending fraudulent emails impersonating Terry Gross, host of the NPR program Fresh Air, to lure authors, entertainers and other public figures into a scheme. The highly personalized messages reference the targets' work and propose interview topics before eventually requesting payment of around $250 for supposed production costs. Misericordia University history professor Jennifer Black received such an email and initially felt excited until she noticed suspicious details like the email coming directly from Gross herself and language that seemed artificially generated. A follow-up request for money confirmed her doubts, and she contacted WHYY security to report the fraud.

Cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams more convincing and affordable than ever before. WHYY, NPR and Fresh Air have confirmed they received complaints about fraudulent emails impersonating Gross and staff members. The organizations state they never charge guests for interviews and advise recipients to verify any interview requests through legitimate contacts. Red flags include requests for payment and emails from unofficial addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com. Similar scams have targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler and journalist Katie Couric.
